title: Model Serving & High-Throughput Inference
description: FastAPI serving, ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, vLLM, PagedAttention, KV-caching, Quantization (AWQ/GPTQ), and SLA percentiles.

sections.title: Production Model Serving & High-Throughput Inference
sections.subtitle: Bridging Research Checkpoints to Sub-Millisecond, Highly Scalable Production Systems

sections.title: The Production Inference Landscape
sections.text: Training optimizes for gradient throughput across static datasets. In production, serving systems optimize for fundamentally different constraints: **Time to First Token (TTFT)**, **Inter-Token Latency (ITL)**, **P99 latency SLAs**, and **Token Throughput per Dollar**. Raw PyTorch models in standard Python servers suffer from Python Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) contention, memory fragmentation, and unoptimized CUDA execution.

sections.title: Inference Optimization & Acceleration Stack
rows: Asynchronous non-blocking event loops, Pydantic validation, concurrent request queueing.
Hardware-agnostic graph fusion (Conv+BN+ReLU $\to$ single kernel), constant folding, dead-node elimination.
Kernel auto-tuning for specific GPU architectures, layer fusion, dynamic tensor memory allocation.
Ultra-low latency computer vision and deep learning inference on NVIDIA GPUs.
Paged virtual memory management for KV-cache, continuous iteration-level batching.
Production multi-user LLM serving (up to 4x higher throughput).
Dynamic batching, concurrent model execution across multiple GPUs, multi-framework support.

sections.title: Weight Quantization Mechanics: Symmetric vs Asymmetric
sections.text:
Quantization maps 32-bit floating point weights ($W \in \mathbb{R}$) to lower-bit integers ($q \in \mathbb{Z}_{\text{int8}}$):

$$q = \text{clip}\left( \left\lfloor \frac{W}{S} \right\rceil + Z, \; q_{min}, \; q_{max} \right)$$

$$\tilde{W} = S \cdot (q - Z)$$

Where $S = \frac{W_{max} - W_{min}}{q_{max} - q_{min}}$ is the **Scale Factor**, and $Z$ is the integer **Zero-Point**.

- **Symmetric Quantization ($Z = 0$):** Constrains scale to $S = \frac{\max(|W|)}{q_{max}}$, saving computation on zero-point additions.
- **Modern LLM Quantization (AWQ / GPTQ):** Compresses 16-bit weights to **INT4** (4 bits per weight), slashing model VRAM by **$75\%$** (e.g. 70B model drops from 140GB to 35GB) with negligible perplexity degradation.

sections.title: Continuous (Iteration-Level) Batching vs Static Batching
sections.body:
- **Static Batching:** Waits for $B$ requests, batches them together, and runs forward passes until all sequences complete. Slowest request bottlenecks the entire batch, leaving GPU cores idle (head-of-line blocking).
- **Continuous Batching (Orca / vLLM):** Operates at the iteration level. As soon as sequence $A$ emits `<EOS>`, it is immediately evicted from the batch and a newly arrived request $D$ is spliced into the vacant slot on the very next token generation step, achieving **$100\%$ GPU core saturation**.

quiz.question: Why is deploying raw PyTorch models directly inside standard Python WSGI servers (e.g. Flask/Gunicorn) suboptimal for high-throughput serving?
options: Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) limits multi-threaded CPU concurrency, and lack of dynamic batching causes poor GPU saturation
PyTorch cannot run outside Jupyter notebooks
Flask deletes model weights on each request
PyTorch only runs on MacOS
quiz.explanation: Python's GIL restricts concurrency and raw PyTorch lacks specialized memory management (like PagedAttention) and dynamic request batching.

quiz.question: What is Time to First Token (TTFT) in LLM serving?
options: The latency from when a user sends a prompt until the model begins streaming the very first generated output token
The time it takes to train the model
The time to download the model from Hugging Face
The time to tokenize the vocabulary
quiz.explanation: TTFT measures the prompt-processing (prefill) latency before generation begins, critical for user-perceived responsiveness.

quiz.question: What is Inter-Token Latency (ITL) or Time Per Output Token (TPOT)?
options: The average time elapsed between generating consecutive output tokens during the autoregressive decoding phase
The time between user keystrokes
The latency of the internet router
The time to shut down the server
quiz.explanation: ITL measures the decoding speed (e.g. 25ms per token = 40 tokens/sec), determining how smoothly text streams to the user.

quiz.question: What is the difference between P50, P95, and P99 latency percentiles?
options: P99 is the latency threshold below which 99% of requests complete, capturing worst-case tail latency spikes for SLA guarantees
P99 is the average latency plus 99ms
P50 is the maximum latency
P95 measures memory usage
quiz.explanation: Percentiles quantify the latency distribution: P50 is median, while P99 captures outlier latency experienced by the slowest 1% of users.

quiz.question: What is Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX)?
options: An open standard format for representing machine learning models that allows exporting models from PyTorch/TensorFlow and running them on diverse runtimes
A stock exchange for AI startups
A networking protocol for GPUs
A dataset of open neural nets
quiz.explanation: ONNX provides an open computational graph representation that decouples training frameworks from production deployment runtimes.

quiz.question: What is Operator Fusion (Kernel Fusion) in inference optimization engines (like ONNX Runtime or TensorRT)?
options: Combining consecutive operations (such as Conv + BatchNorm + ReLU) into a single fused GPU kernel to eliminate redundant memory read/write passes to global VRAM
Fusing two models into one
Connecting two GPUs with a physical wire
Merging two Python scripts
quiz.explanation: Kernel fusion executes sequential operations in on-chip GPU registers/SRAM, avoiding expensive round-trips to high-bandwidth global memory.

quiz.question: What is NVIDIA TensorRT?
options: An inference compiler and runtime that optimizes neural networks specifically for NVIDIA GPUs via layer fusion, precision calibration, and kernel auto-tuning
A library for training deep networks on CPUs
A 3D rendering engine for games
A tensor database
quiz.explanation: TensorRT compiles models directly into hardware-optimized binary execution plans for specific GPU architectures.

quiz.question: What is Constant Folding in graph compilation?
options: Pre-computing operations that involve only compile-time constants so they do not execute at runtime during inference
Folding weights like paper to save space
Setting all constants to zero
Compressing constants with zip
quiz.explanation: Constant folding simplifies graph nodes whose inputs are static at build time, eliminating unnecessary runtime computation.

quiz.question: What is Continuous Batching (Iteration-Level Batching, Orca / vLLM)?
options: Dynamically inserting new incoming requests and evicting completed sequences at every individual token decoding step rather than waiting for an entire batch to finish
Batching data continuously for 24 hours
Processing one token per day
Training while serving simultaneously
quiz.explanation: Continuous batching eliminates idle GPU capacity caused by varying request lengths, dramatically increasing serving throughput.

quiz.question: How does PagedAttention (vLLM) resolve the memory waste of standard KV-caching?
options: By storing KV cache states in non-contiguous virtual memory blocks (pages), eliminating internal memory fragmentation and pre-allocation waste
By paging GPU memory to the hard drive
By compressing tokens into 1-bit codes
By deleting old tokens from cache
quiz.explanation: Traditional serving pre-allocates contiguous memory for maximum sequence lengths, wasting 60-80% of VRAM; PagedAttention allocates blocks dynamically on-demand.

quiz.question: What is Weight-Only Quantization vs Weight-and-Activation Quantization?
options: Weight-only (e.g. W4A16) quantizes stored weights while computing matmuls in FP16; weight-and-activation (W8A8) quantizes both, using fast INT8 tensor cores
Weight-only only works on CPUs
Weight-and-activation deletes activations
Weight-only doubles memory usage
quiz.explanation: Weight-only quantization saves memory bandwidth for memory-bound decoding; W8A8 accelerates compute-bound operations using INT8 GEMM kernels.

quiz.question: What is AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization, Lin et al., 2023)?
options: Protecting the 1% most salient weights (identified by observing activation magnitudes) by scaling them up before quantizing remaining weights to INT4
An audio quantization algorithm
A tool for automatic weight pruning
A quantization scheme for web servers
quiz.explanation: AWQ preserves the critical top 1% outlier weights that protect perplexity while quantizing the remaining 99% of weights to 4 bits.

quiz.question: What is GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022)?
options: A one-shot weight quantization method based on Approximate Second-Order Information (Hessian inverse) that quantizes weights to 3-bit or 4-bit in a few GPU hours
A language model developed by OpenAI
A queue system for GPT models
A method for generating text queries
quiz.explanation: GPTQ solves an optimal brain surgeon error minimization problem using inverse Hessians to quantize 175B models accurately in minimal time.

quiz.question: What is Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) vs Quantization-Aware Training (QAT)?
options: PTQ quantizes weights after training without full retraining; QAT models quantization errors during training using fake-quantization operators
PTQ requires 100 GPUs; QAT requires none
QAT is only for vision models
PTQ converts models to C++
quiz.explanation: PTQ is fast and requires only a small calibration dataset; QAT simulates quantization noise during backprop to achieve maximum accuracy at low bit-widths (e.g. INT4).

quiz.question: What is Dynamic Batching in model serving (e.g. Triton Inference Server)?
options: Aggregating individual client requests that arrive within a short time window (e.g. 5ms) into a single batch to maximize GPU parallelism
Changing batch size randomly during inference
Running batch jobs at midnight
Splitting a request across multiple users
quiz.explanation: Dynamic batching buffers incoming concurrent requests up to a max queue delay, combining them into efficient batched matrix operations.

quiz.question: What is Tensor Parallelism (Megatron-LM, Shoeybi et al.)?
options: Splitting individual weight matrices (such as attention projections) across multiple GPUs within the same server node via high-speed NVLink interconnects
Running multiple models on one GPU
Running PyTorch on tensors
Splitting batches across different nodes
quiz.explanation: Tensor parallelism partitions large matrix multiplications (column-parallel and row-parallel) across GPUs connected by NVLink for ultra-fast intra-node execution.

quiz.question: What is Pipeline Parallelism (GPipe / Megatron-LM)?
options: Partitioning the sequential layers of a deep network across different GPU devices, passing intermediate activations forward and backward along a pipeline
Piping Unix shell commands into Python
Running data through a physical water pipe
Connecting GPUs with Ethernet cables
quiz.explanation: Pipeline parallelism assigns blocks of consecutive layers to different GPUs, managing execution bubbles via micro-batching.

quiz.question: What is Data Parallelism (DDP) in distributed ML?
options: Replicating the entire model on every GPU, feeding each GPU a distinct slice of the mini-batch, and synchronizing gradients via All-Reduce
Storing data on multiple hard drives
Splitting database tables across tables
Copying the dataset 100 times
quiz.explanation: DistributedDataParallel (DDP) replicates model weights across workers, executing parallel forward passes and synchronizing gradients with Ring AllReduce.

quiz.question: What is ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer, Rajbhandari et al., DeepSpeed)?
options: Eliminating memory redundancy in data parallelism by sharding optimizer states (Stage 1), gradients (Stage 2), and model parameters (Stage 3) across GPUs
An optimizer with zero learning rate
A model with zero parameters
A library for running models on zero GPUs
quiz.explanation: DeepSpeed ZeRO removes the duplicate memory footprint of data parallelism by partitioning optimizer states, gradients, and parameters across workers.

quiz.question: What is FlashDecoding / FlashDecoding++?
options: Optimizing attention decoding for long contexts by parallelizing the reduction across the sequence length dimension in addition to batch and head dimensions
A flash drive for storing models
Decoding text in Adobe Flash
Compressing output tokens
quiz.explanation: While FlashAttention parallelizes across batch and heads, FlashDecoding parallelizes across the keys/values sequence dimension, speeding up long-context generation by up to 8x.

quiz.question: What is Speculative Decoding?
options: Drafting K tokens quickly using a smaller draft model and verifying them simultaneously in a single forward pass of the large target model
Guessing what the user will type next
Evaluating models with speculative investments
Sampling tokens with high temperature
quiz.explanation: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by turning K sequential passes into 1 parallel verification pass for accepted tokens.

quiz.question: What is Model Pruning (Magnitude Pruning)?
options: Setting small weight values below a threshold to zero and converting dense tensors into sparse matrices to reduce memory and compute
Deleting old model checkpoints from disk
Removing comments from code
Cutting model training time in half
quiz.explanation: Magnitude pruning removes insignificant weights whose absolute values are close to zero, creating sparse networks.

quiz.question: What is Structured Pruning vs Unstructured Pruning?
options: Structured pruning removes entire channels, attention heads, or layers, yielding direct hardware speedups without sparse matrix libraries; unstructured zeros individual weights
Structured pruning is for SQL databases; unstructured is for text
Unstructured pruning is faster on GPUs
They are identical
quiz.explanation: Structured pruning removes complete hardware blocks (e.g. 20% of channels), running efficiently on standard dense matrix hardware.

quiz.question: What is Knowledge Distillation for model compression?
options: Training a compact student network to match the probability distribution and latent features of a massive teacher model
Boiling data to remove noise
Saving model weights in a zip file
Extracting text from a PDF
quiz.explanation: Knowledge distillation compresses a huge model (e.g. 70B teacher) into a nimble model (e.g. 7B student) with minimal degradation.

quiz.question: What is Triton Inference Server (NVIDIA)?
options: An enterprise open-source model serving software that supports multiple framework backends, concurrent models, dynamic batching, and GPU metrics
A programming language developed by OpenAI
A GPU hardware card
An operating system for supercomputers
quiz.explanation: NVIDIA Triton provides unified production serving for PyTorch, TensorRT, ONNX, and vLLM backends with dynamic batching and autoscaling.

quiz.question: In high-throughput serving, what does 'GPU Compute Bound' vs 'GPU Memory Bandwidth Bound' mean?
options: Compute bound means the arithmetic processing units (Tensor Cores) are saturated; memory bandwidth bound means execution waits on transferring weights from VRAM to SRAM
Compute bound means the CPU is slow
Memory bound means hard drive is full
They mean the same thing
quiz.explanation: Prefill (prompt processing) is compute-bound (massive parallel matrix multiplication); autoregressive decoding is memory-bandwidth bound (reading gigabytes of weights for 1 token).

quiz.question: Why is autoregressive token generation in LLMs predominantly Memory Bandwidth Bound?
options: Generating each single token requires loading the entire model's multi-gigabyte weight tensors from VRAM into the compute cores for just one matrix-vector product
Because tokens are very long strings
Because GPUs lack memory
Because Python is slow
quiz.explanation: Each token requires reading billions of parameters from VRAM (e.g. 14GB for 7B FP16) to perform minimal arithmetic for one token, capping speed by memory bus bandwidth.

quiz.question: What is Prefix Caching (Prompt Caching) in LLM inference engines?
options: Reusing the computed KV cache of common prompt prefixes (system instructions, multi-shot examples, large documents) across multiple requests
Caching website URLs
Saving user passwords in cache
Storing tokens in Redis
quiz.explanation: Prefix caching skips the compute-heavy prefill phase for shared system prompts, drastically reducing TTFT and cutting compute costs by up to 80%.

quiz.question: What is Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) input detection in production serving?
options: A monitoring mechanism that flags incoming inference queries whose feature distribution deviates significantly from the training distribution
Detecting requests from foreign countries
Detecting corrupted JSON syntax
Detecting requests that timeout
quiz.explanation: OOD detectors identify anomalous queries where the model's predictions are likely unreliable or severely miscalibrated.

quiz.question: What is A/B Testing in machine learning deployment?
options: Splitting live user traffic between model version A and model version B to statistically compare business and operational metrics
Testing models on datasets A and B locally
Testing with two different Python versions
Testing on AMD vs NVIDIA GPUs
quiz.explanation: A/B testing routes a fraction of production traffic to candidate models to rigorously measure performance differences on real users.

quiz.question: What is Shadow Deployment (Dark Launching)?
options: Routing live production requests to a new candidate model in the background without returning its outputs to users, evaluating its latency and accuracy safely
Deploying models at night
Deploying models in stealth mode to avoid hackers
Running models with black backgrounds
quiz.explanation: Shadow deployment tests real-world operational load and output quality with zero risk of user-facing errors.

quiz.question: What is Canary Deployment in ML operations?
options: Gradually rolling out a new model version to a tiny percentage of users (e.g. 2%), monitoring errors/latency before rolling out to 100%
Using a canary bird in the datacenter
Testing models on bird recognition datasets
Deploying models on yellow servers
quiz.explanation: Canary releases limit blast radius if a newly deployed model contains unexpected regressions or memory leaks.

quiz.question: What is gRPC and why is it frequently preferred over REST for internal microservice ML inference?
options: gRPC uses HTTP/2 with binary protocol buffers (Protobuf), providing significantly lower serialization overhead and faster streaming than text-based JSON REST
gRPC is easier to read in a browser
gRPC only works with Python
gRPC does not require network connections
quiz.explanation: Protobuf binary serialization and multiplexed HTTP/2 streaming make gRPC substantially faster and more efficient for high-frequency model calls.

quiz.question: What is Circuit Breaking in an inference serving architecture?
options: An architectural pattern that automatically stops sending requests to a degraded or failing backend service, returning fallbacks to prevent cascading system failures
Cutting physical power cords to servers
Breaking encryption keys
Halting training when loss plateaus
quiz.explanation: Circuit breakers detect failing model replicas and fail fast or route to fallback caches, protecting upstream microservices.

quiz.question: What is Graceful Degradation in an ML serving system?
options: Falling back to a faster, smaller model or cached heuristic responses when the primary heavy model cluster is overloaded or experiencing failures
Letting servers crash cleanly
Slowly deleting model weights
Lowering screen resolution for users
quiz.explanation: Graceful degradation ensures the system remains functional under extreme traffic spikes rather than suffering total outage.
